title: Book 3, Chapter 11 — Year of the War—Campaigns of Demosthenes in Western Greece—Ruin of Ambracia
paragraphs: Summer was now over. The following winter the plague struck the Athenians a second time. It had never entirely left them, but there had been a noticeable lull in its ravages. The second visit lasted no less than a year, the first having lasted two; and nothing distressed the Athenians or weakened their power more. No fewer than four thousand four hundred heavy infantry in the ranks died of it, three hundred cavalry, and an unknown number of the common multitude. At the same time came the numerous earthquakes in Athens, Euboea, and Boeotia, particularly at Orchomenus in Boeotia.

The same winter the Athenians in Sicily and the Rhegians, with thirty ships, made an expedition against the islands of Aeolus, which cannot be invaded in summer because of the lack of water. These islands are held by the Liparaeans, a Cnidian colony, who live in one of them — Lipara, which is not large — and from this as their headquarters work the rest, Didyme, Strongyle, and Hiera. On Hiera the people in those parts believe that Hephaestus has his forge, from the amount of flame they see it send out by night and the smoke by day. These islands lie off the coast of the Sicels and Messenians and were allies of the Syracusans. The Athenians laid waste their land, and as the inhabitants would not submit, sailed back to Rhegium. So the winter ended, and with it the fifth year of this war of which Thucydides was the historian.

The next summer the Peloponnesians and their allies set out to invade Attica under the command of Agis, son of Archidamus. They got as far as the Isthmus, but with numerous earthquakes occurring, they turned back without invading. About the same time as these earthquakes were so frequent, the sea at Orobiae in Euboea retreated from the existing line of coast and then returned in a huge wave, swept over a great part of the town, and withdrew, leaving some of it still under water; what was once land is now sea. Those of the inhabitants who could not run up to higher ground in time perished. A similar inundation happened at Atalanta, the island off the Opuntian Locrian coast, carrying away part of the Athenian fort and wrecking one of two ships drawn up on the beach. At Peparethus too the sea retreated a little, but no flood followed; an earthquake threw down part of the wall, the town hall, and a few other buildings. The cause of this phenomenon, in my opinion, must be sought in the earthquake. At the point where its shock has been most violent, the sea is driven back, and then, recoiling suddenly with redoubled force, causes the inundation. Without an earthquake I do not see how such a thing could happen.

During the same summer the various belligerents in Sicily carried on different operations: the Sicilians among themselves, and the Athenians and their allies. I will, however, confine myself to the actions in which the Athenians took part, choosing the most important. After the death of the Athenian general Charoeades, killed by the Syracusans in battle, Laches was left in sole command of the fleet, which he now directed in concert with the allies against Mylae, a town belonging to the Messenians. Two Messenian battalions in garrison at Mylae set an ambush for the party landing from the ships, but were routed with great slaughter by the Athenians and their allies, who then assaulted the fortification and forced them to surrender the acropolis and march with them against Messina. This town also submitted afterwards on the approach of the Athenians and their allies, and gave hostages and all other securities required.

The same summer the Athenians sent thirty ships round the Peloponnese under Demosthenes, son of Alcisthenes, and Procles, son of Theodorus, and sixty more, with two thousand heavy infantry, against Melos under Nicias, son of Niceratus. They wanted to reduce the Melians, who, although islanders, refused to be subjects of Athens or even to join her confederacy. The devastation of their land did not bring them to terms, so the fleet weighed from Melos and sailed to Oropus in the territory of Graea. Landing at nightfall, the heavy infantry started at once from the ships by land for Tanagra in Boeotia, where they were met, by prearranged signal, by the whole levy from Athens, under Hipponicus, son of Callias, and Eurymedon, son of Thucles. They encamped, and after spending that day ravaging the territory of Tanagra, stayed there for the night. The next day, after defeating those of the Tanagraeans who came out against them and some Thebans who had come up to help them, they took some arms, set up a trophy, and withdrew — the troops to the city, the rest to the ships. Nicias, with his sixty ships, coasted along the shore, ravaged the Locrian seaboard, and so returned home.

About this time the Lacedaemonians founded their colony of Heraclea in Trachis, with this object in view. The Malians form three tribes in all — the Paralians, the Hiereans, and the Trachinians. The Trachinians, having suffered severely in a war with their neighbours the Oetaeans, at first intended to put themselves under Athens; but afterwards, fearing they would not find with her the security they sought, they sent to Lacedaemon, having chosen Tisamenus as their ambassador. The Dorians, from the mother country of the Lacedaemonians, joined this embassy with the same request, since they too were suffering from the same enemy. After hearing them, the Lacedaemonians decided to send out the colony, both to help the Trachinians and Dorians and because they thought the proposed town would lie conveniently for the war against the Athenians. A fleet might be readied there against Euboea, with the advantage of a short crossing to the island; and the town would also be useful as a station on the road to Thrace. In short, everything made the Lacedaemonians eager to found the place. After first consulting the god at Delphi and getting a favourable answer, they sent off the colonists, Spartans and Perioeci, also inviting any of the rest of the Hellenes who wished to join, except Ionians, Achaeans, and certain other peoples. Three Lacedaemonians led as founders of the colony — Leon, Alcidas, and Damagon. With the settlement made, they freshly fortified the city, now called Heraclea, about four and a half miles from Thermopylae and two and a quarter from the sea, and began building docks, closing the side toward Thermopylae just at the pass itself, so that they could be easily defended.

The foundation of this town, evidently meant to harass Euboea (the crossing to Cenaeum on the island being a short one), at first caused some alarm at Athens, which the event, however, did nothing to justify, since the town never gave them any trouble. The reason was this. The Thessalians, who held sway in those parts and whose territory was threatened by its foundation, were afraid it might prove a powerful neighbour and so continually harassed and made war on the new settlers, until at last they wore them out, in spite of their originally considerable numbers — people had flocked from all quarters to a place founded by the Lacedaemonians and so thought sure of prosperity. On the other hand, the Lacedaemonians themselves, in the persons of their governors, did their full share towards ruining its prosperity and reducing its population, since they frightened away most of the inhabitants by governing harshly and in some cases unfairly, and so made it easier for their neighbours to prevail against them.

The same summer, around the time the Athenians were detained at Melos, their fellow citizens in the thirty ships cruising round the Peloponnese, after cutting off some guards in an ambush at Ellomenus in Leucadia, then went against Leucas itself with a large force, having been reinforced by the whole levy of the Acarnanians except Oeniadae, by the Zacynthians and Cephallenians, and by fifteen ships from Corcyra. While the Leucadians watched the devastation of their land, both outside and inside the isthmus on which the town of Leucas and the temple of Apollo stand, they made no move because of the overwhelming numbers of the enemy. The Acarnanians urged Demosthenes, the Athenian general, to build a wall to cut the town off from the mainland — a measure they were sure would secure its capture and rid them once and for all of a most troublesome enemy.

Demosthenes, however, had meanwhile been persuaded by the Messenians that this was a fine opportunity, with so large an army assembled, to attack the Aetolians, who were not only the enemies of Naupactus, but whose reduction would also make it easy to gain the rest of that part of the mainland for the Athenians. The Aetolian nation, although numerous and warlike, lived in unwalled villages scattered far apart and had nothing but light arms; according to the Messenians, they could be subdued without much difficulty before reinforcements could arrive. The plan they recommended was to attack first the Apodotians, then the Ophionians, and after them the Eurytanians, who are the largest tribe in Aetolia and speak, it is said, an extremely difficult language and eat their flesh raw. Once these were subdued, the rest would easily come in.

Demosthenes consented to this plan, both to please the Messenians and in the belief that, by adding the Aetolians to his other mainland allies, he would be able, without help from home, to march against the Boeotians by way of Ozolian Locris to Kytinium in Doris, keeping Parnassus on his right until he descended on the Phocians, whom he could compel to join him if their old friendship for Athens did not, as he expected, immediately decide them to do so. Once in Phocis he was already on the frontier of Boeotia. He accordingly weighed from Leucas, against the wish of the Acarnanians, and with his whole force sailed along the coast to Sollium, where he disclosed his plan to them. When they refused to agree, because of the failure to invest Leucas, he set out on his expedition against the Aetolians with the rest of the forces — the Cephallenians, the Messenians, the Zacynthians, and three hundred Athenian marines from his own ships (the fifteen Corcyraean ships had departed). He established his base at Oeneon in Locris, since the Ozolian Locrians were allies of Athens and were to meet him with all their forces in the interior. Being neighbours of the Aetolians and armed in the same way, they were thought likely to be of great service on the expedition, given their familiarity with the country and the way the inhabitants fought.

After bivouacking with the army in the precinct of Nemean Zeus, where the poet Hesiod is said to have been killed by the people of the country, in fulfilment of an oracle that had foretold he would die at Nemea, Demosthenes set out at daybreak to invade Aetolia. The first day he took Potidania, the next Krokyle, and the third Tichium, where he halted and sent the booty back to Eupalium in Locris, having decided to push his conquests as far as the Ophionians and, if they refused to submit, to return to Naupactus and make them the object of a second expedition. Meanwhile the Aetolians had been aware of his plan from the moment it was formed, and as soon as the army invaded their country they came up in great force with all their tribes — even the most remote Ophionians, the Bomiensians, and Calliensians, who extend toward the Malian Gulf, were among them.

The Messenians, however, stuck to their original advice. Assuring Demosthenes that the Aetolians were an easy conquest, they urged him to push on as fast as possible and to try to take the villages as fast as he came to them, not waiting until the whole nation was in arms against him. Led on by his advisers and trusting in his luck, since he had met no opposition, and without waiting for his Locrian reinforcements — who were to have supplied him with the light-armed darters in which he was most lacking — he advanced and stormed Aegitium. The inhabitants fled before him and posted themselves on the hills above the town, which stood on high ground about nine miles from the sea. Meanwhile the Aetolians had gathered to the rescue and now attacked the Athenians and their allies, running down from the hills on every side and hurling their javelins, falling back when the Athenian army advanced, and pressing on as it retired. For a long time the battle went on like this, advance and retreat in turn, with the Athenians getting the worse of both.

Still, as long as their archers had arrows left and could use them, they held out, the light-armed Aetolians retreating before the arrows; but after the captain of the archers had been killed and his men scattered, the soldiers, worn out by the constant repetition of the same exertions and hard pressed by the Aetolians with their javelins, at last turned and fled. Falling into trackless gullies and places they did not know, they perished there; their guide, the Messenian Chromon, having unfortunately also been killed. A great many were overtaken in the pursuit by the swift-footed light-armed Aetolians and fell beneath their javelins; but most missed their way and rushed into the wood, which had no exit, and which the enemy soon set on fire and burnt round them. The Athenian army fell victims to death in every form, and went through every hardship of flight; the survivors with difficulty escaped to the sea and to Oeneon in Locris, where they had set out from. Many of the allies were killed, and about one hundred and twenty Athenian heavy infantry — not a man less, all in the prime of life. These were by far the best men of the city of Athens to fall during this war. Among the slain was also Procles, the colleague of Demosthenes. The Athenians took up their dead under truce from the Aetolians and withdrew to Naupactus, and from there sailed in their ships to Athens; Demosthenes stayed behind in Naupactus and the surrounding area, afraid to face the Athenians after the disaster.
About the same time the Athenians on the coast of Sicily sailed to Locris, and in a landing they made from the ships defeated the Locrians who came against them and took a fort on the river Halex.

The same summer the Aetolians, who before the Athenian expedition had sent an embassy to Corinth and Lacedaemon — composed of Tolophus, an Ophionian, Boriades, an Eurytanian, and Tisander, an Apodotian — obtained an army to be sent to them against Naupactus, which had brought on the Athenian invasion. The Lacedaemonians accordingly sent off, towards autumn, three thousand allied heavy infantry, five hundred of whom were from Heraclea, the newly founded city in Trachis, under the command of Eurylochus, a Spartan, accompanied by Macarius and Menedaius, also Spartans.

After the army had assembled at Delphi, Eurylochus sent a herald to the Ozolian Locrians, since the road to Naupactus lay through their territory and he had also conceived the idea of detaching them from Athens. His chief supporters in Locris were the Amphissians, alarmed at the hostility of the Phocians. They were the first to give hostages themselves and persuaded the rest to do the same out of fear of the invading army — first their neighbours the Myonians, who held the most difficult of the passes, and after them the Ipnians, Messapians, Tritaeans, Chalaeans, Tolophonians, Hessians, and Oeanthians, all of whom joined the expedition. The Olpaeans contented themselves with giving hostages without joining the invasion, while the Hyaeans refused to do either, until the capture of Polis, one of their villages.

His preparations complete, Eurylochus lodged the hostages in Kytinium, in Doris, and advanced upon Naupactus through the country of the Locrians, taking on his way Oeneon and Eupalium, two of their towns that refused to join him. Once in Naupactian territory, and now joined by the Aetolians, the army laid waste the land and took the suburb of the town, which was unfortified, and after this Molycrium too, a Corinthian colony subject to Athens. Meanwhile the Athenian Demosthenes, who since the affair in Aetolia had remained near Naupactus, having had word of the army and fearing for the town, went and persuaded the Acarnanians, although not without difficulty because he had left Leucas, to relieve Naupactus. They accordingly sent with him on board his ships a thousand heavy infantry, who threw themselves into the place and saved it; otherwise the extent of its wall and the small number of its defenders had put it in the greatest danger. Meanwhile Eurylochus and his companions, finding that this force had got in and that storming the town was impossible, withdrew, not to the Peloponnese, but to the country once called Aeolis and now Calydon and Pleuron, and to the places in that area, and to Proschium in Aetolia. The Ambraciots had come and urged them to combine with them in attacking Amphilochian Argos and the rest of Amphilochia and Acarnania, claiming that the conquest of these countries would bring all the mainland into alliance with Lacedaemon. Eurylochus consented to this, and dismissing the Aetolians, now stayed quiet with his army in those parts, until the time should come for the Ambraciots to take the field and for him to join them before Argos.

Summer was now over. The following winter the Athenians in Sicily, with their Hellenic allies and those of the Sicel subjects or allies of Syracuse who had revolted from her and joined their army, marched against the Sicel town of Inessa, the acropolis of which was held by the Syracusans. After attacking it without being able to take it, they retired. In the retreat the allies, marching after the Athenians, were attacked by the Syracusans from the fort, and a large part of their army was routed with great slaughter. After this Laches and the Athenians from the ships made some landings in Locris and, defeating the Locrians who came against them with Proxenus, son of Capaton, on the river Caicinus, took some arms and departed.

The same winter the Athenians purified Delos, in compliance, it appears, with a certain oracle. It had been purified before by Pisistratus the tyrant — not the whole island, but as much of it as could be seen from the temple. Now, however, the whole was purified in the following way. All the sepulchres of those who had died on Delos were taken up, and for the future it was ordered that no one was to be allowed to die or give birth to a child on the island; they were to be carried over to Rhenea, which is so close to Delos that Polycrates, tyrant of Samos, having added Rhenea to his other island conquests during his period of naval supremacy, dedicated it to the Delian Apollo by binding it to Delos with a chain.

After the purification, the Athenians celebrated for the first time the quinquennial festival of the Delian games. There had once been, indeed, a great gathering of the Ionians and the neighbouring islanders at Delos, who used to come to the festival as the Ionians now do to that of Ephesus; athletic and poetical contests took place there, and the cities brought choirs of dancers. Nothing can be clearer on this point than the following lines of Homer, taken from a hymn to Apollo:

Phœbus, wherever thou strayest, far or near, Delos was still of all thy haunts most dear. Thither the robed Ionians take their way With wife and child to keep thy holiday, Invoke thy favour on each manly game, And dance and sing in honour of thy name.

That there was also a poetical contest in which the Ionians went to compete is shown by the following, taken from the same hymn. After praising the Delian dance of the women, he ends his song of praise with these lines, in which he also alludes to himself:

Well, may Apollo keep you all! and so, Sweethearts, good-bye — yet tell me not I go Out from your hearts; and if in after hours Some other wanderer in this world of ours Touch at your shores, and ask your maidens here Who sings the songs the sweetest to your ear, Think of me then, and answer with a smile, ‘A blind old man of Scio’s rocky isle.’

Homer thus attests that there was once a great assembly and festival at Delos. In later times, although the islanders and the Athenians continued to send the choirs of dancers with sacrifices, the contests and most of the ceremonies were abolished, probably through hardship, until the Athenians on this occasion celebrated the games with the novelty of horse-races.

The same winter the Ambraciots, as they had promised Eurylochus when they retained his army, marched out against Amphilochian Argos with three thousand heavy infantry, and invading Argive territory occupied Olpae, a stronghold on a hill near the sea, formerly fortified by the Acarnanians and used as the place of assizes for their nation, about two and three-quarters miles from the city of Argos on the seacoast. Meanwhile the Acarnanians went with part of their forces to relieve Argos, and with the rest encamped in Amphilochia at the place called Crenae, or the Wells, to watch for Eurylochus and his Peloponnesians and prevent them from passing through and joining up with the Ambraciots. They also sent for Demosthenes, the commander of the Aetolian expedition, to be their leader, and for the twenty Athenian ships cruising off the Peloponnese under the command of Aristotle, son of Timocrates, and Hierophon, son of Antimnestus. The Ambraciots at Olpae, on their part, sent a messenger to their own city begging them to come with their full levy to their aid, fearing that Eurylochus’s army might not be able to push through the Acarnanians, and that they themselves might be forced to fight alone, or be unable to retreat without danger if they wished to.

Meanwhile Eurylochus and his Peloponnesians, learning that the Ambraciots at Olpae had arrived, set out from Proschium in all haste to join them. Crossing the Achelous, they advanced through Acarnania, which they found deserted by its population, who had gone to relieve Argos. They kept on their right the city of the Stratians and its garrison, and on their left the rest of Acarnania. Crossing the territory of the Stratians, they advanced through Phytia, then, skirting Medeon, through Limnaea; after which they left Acarnania behind and entered friendly country — that of the Agraeans. From there they reached and crossed Mount Thymaus, which belongs to the Agraeans, and descended into Argive territory after nightfall, and passing between the city of Argos and the Acarnanian posts at Crenae, joined the Ambraciots at Olpae.

Joining up here at daybreak, they sat down at the place called Metropolis and made camp. Not long after, the Athenians in the twenty ships came into the Ambracian Gulf to support the Argives, with Demosthenes and two hundred Messenian heavy infantry and sixty Athenian archers. While the fleet off Olpae blockaded the hill from the sea, the Acarnanians and a few of the Amphilochians — most of whom were held back by force by the Ambraciots — had already arrived at Argos and were preparing to give battle to the enemy, having chosen Demosthenes to command the whole of the allied army together with their own generals. Demosthenes led them up close to Olpae and encamped, with a great ravine separating the two armies. For five days they stayed inactive; on the sixth, both sides drew up in order of battle. The Peloponnesian army was the larger and outflanked their opponents; and Demosthenes, fearing that his right might be surrounded, posted in ambush in a hollow road overgrown with bushes some four hundred heavy infantry and light troops, who were to rise up at the moment of the onset behind the projecting left wing of the enemy and take them in the rear. When both sides were ready they joined battle. Demosthenes was on the right wing with the Messenians and a few Athenians, while the rest of the line was made up of the various divisions of the Acarnanians and of the Amphilochian darters. The Peloponnesians and Ambraciots were drawn up mixed together, except for the Mantineans, who were massed on the left, though not reaching to the very end of the wing, where Eurylochus and his men confronted the Messenians and Demosthenes.

The Peloponnesians, now well engaged, were just on the point of turning their enemy’s right with their outflanking wing, when the Acarnanians from the ambush set on them from behind and broke them at the first attack, without their staying to resist; the panic into which they fell caused the flight of most of their army, terrified beyond measure at seeing the division of Eurylochus and their best troops cut to pieces. Most of the work was done by Demosthenes and his Messenians, who were posted in this part of the field. Meanwhile the Ambraciots — the best soldiers in those countries — and the troops on the right wing defeated the division facing them and pursued it as far as Argos. Returning from the pursuit, they found their main body defeated; and hard pressed by the Acarnanians, with difficulty made their way through to Olpae, suffering heavy loss along the way as they dashed on without discipline or order — except for the Mantineans, who kept their ranks better than any other unit in the army during the retreat.

The battle did not end until evening. The next day Menedaius, who on the death of Eurylochus and Macarius had succeeded to sole command, was at a loss after such a signal defeat as to how to stay and stand a siege, cut off as he was on land and by the Athenian fleet at sea, and equally how to retreat in safety. He opened a parley with Demosthenes and the Acarnanian generals for a truce and permission to withdraw, and at the same time for the recovery of the dead. The dead they gave back, and after setting up a trophy they took up their own as well, about three hundred in number. The retreat asked for they refused publicly to the army; but permission to depart at once was secretly granted to the Mantineans and to Menedaius and the other commanders and leading men of the Peloponnesians by Demosthenes and his Acarnanian colleagues, who wanted to strip the Ambraciots and the mercenary host of foreigners of their supporters and, above all, to discredit the Lacedaemonians and Peloponnesians with the Hellenes in those parts as traitors and self-seekers.

While the enemy was taking up his dead and hastily burying them as best he could, and those who had gained permission were secretly arranging their retreat, word was brought to Demosthenes and the Acarnanians that the Ambraciots from the city, in compliance with the first message from Olpae, were on the march with their whole levy through Amphilochia to join their countrymen at Olpae, knowing nothing of what had happened. Demosthenes prepared to march out against them with his army, and meanwhile sent on at once a strong division to seize the roads and occupy the strong positions. In the meantime the Mantineans and others included in the agreement went out under the pretence of gathering herbs and firewood and slipped off in twos and threes, picking on the way the things they had pretended to come out for, until they had gone some distance from Olpae, when they quickened their pace. The Ambraciots and others who had accompanied them in larger parties, seeing them going on, pushed on in their turn and started running to catch up. The Acarnanians at first thought all alike were going off without permission and started to chase the Peloponnesians; believing they were being betrayed, they even threw a javelin or two at some of their generals who tried to stop them and explained that leave had been granted. In the end, however, they let the Mantineans and Peloponnesians pass, and killed only the Ambraciots — though there was much dispute and difficulty in telling whether a man was an Ambraciot or a Peloponnesian. The number killed in this way was about two hundred; the rest escaped into the bordering territory of Agraea and found refuge with Salynthius, the friendly king of the Agraeans.

Meanwhile the Ambraciots from the city reached Idomene. Idomene consists of two lofty hills, the higher of which the troops sent on by Demosthenes succeeded in occupying after nightfall, unobserved by the Ambraciots, who had meanwhile climbed the lower one and bivouacked under it. After supper Demosthenes set out with the rest of the army, as soon as it was evening: he himself with half his force made for the pass, while the rest went by way of the Amphilochian hills. At dawn he fell on the Ambraciots while they were still in bed, ignorant of what had happened, and fully thinking these were their own countrymen — Demosthenes having deliberately put the Messenians at the front with orders to address them in the Doric dialect and so inspire confidence in the sentries, who could not see them clearly since it was still dark. In this way he routed their army as soon as he attacked, killing most of them where they lay; the rest broke away in flight over the hills. The roads, however, were already occupied; and while the Amphilochians knew their own country, the Ambraciots did not and could not tell which way to turn, and besides they had heavy armour against a light-armed enemy. So they fell into ravines and into the ambushes that had been set for them, and perished there. In their many efforts to escape, some even turned to the sea, which was not far off, and seeing the Athenian ships coasting along the shore just while the action was going on, swam off to them, thinking it better in their panic to perish, if perish they must, by the hands of the Athenians than at those of the barbarous and detested Amphilochians. Of the great Ambraciot force destroyed in this way, only a few reached the city in safety; while the Acarnanians, after stripping the dead and setting up a trophy, returned to Argos.

The next day a herald arrived from the Ambraciots who had fled from Olpae to the Agraeans, asking leave to take up the dead that had fallen after the first engagement, when they had left the camp with the Mantineans and their companions, without, like them, having had permission. At the sight of the arms of the Ambraciots from the city, the herald was astonished at their number, knowing nothing of the disaster and imagining they belonged to his own party. Someone asked him what he was so astonished at, and how many of them had been killed — imagining, in his turn, that this was the herald from the troops at Idomene. He answered, “About two hundred”; at which his questioner cut him off, saying, “Why, the arms you see here are of more than a thousand.” The herald replied, “Then they are not the arms of those who fought with us?” The other answered, “Yes they are, if at least you fought at Idomene yesterday.” “But we fought no one yesterday; the day before, in the retreat.” “However that may be, we fought yesterday with those who came to reinforce you from the city of the Ambraciots.” When the herald heard this and realized that the reinforcement from the city had been wiped out, he broke into wailing and, stunned at the magnitude of the present evils, went away at once without performing his errand or asking again for the dead bodies. This was by far the greatest disaster that befell any single Hellenic city in the same number of days during this war; and I have not set down the number of the dead, since the figure given seems out of proportion to the size of the city, to the point of being incredible. In any case I know that, had the Acarnanians and Amphilochians wished to take Ambracia as the Athenians and Demosthenes advised, they could have done so without a blow; as it was, they feared that if the Athenians had it, they would be worse neighbours to them than the present ones.

After this the Acarnanians allotted a third of the spoils to the Athenians and divided the rest among their own different towns. The Athenians’ share was captured on the voyage home; the arms now deposited in the Attic temples are the three hundred panoplies which the Acarnanians set apart for Demosthenes, and which he brought to Athens in person — his return home after the Aetolian disaster being made less hazardous by this exploit. The Athenians in the twenty ships also went off to Naupactus. The Acarnanians and Amphilochians, after Demosthenes and the Athenians had departed, granted the Ambraciots and Peloponnesians who had taken refuge with Salynthius and the Agraeans a free withdrawal from Oeniadae, to which they had moved from Salynthius’ country, and for the future concluded a treaty and alliance with the Ambraciots for one hundred years on the following terms. It was to be a defensive alliance, not an offensive one: the Ambraciots could not be required to march with the Acarnanians against the Peloponnesians, nor the Acarnanians with the Ambraciots against the Athenians; for the rest, the Ambraciots were to give up the places and hostages they held of the Amphilochians, and not to give help to Anactorium, which was at odds with the Acarnanians. With this arrangement they put an end to the war. After this the Corinthians sent a garrison of their own citizens to Ambracia — three hundred heavy infantry under the command of Xenocleides, son of Euthycles, who reached their destination after a difficult journey overland. Such was the history of the Ambracia affair.

The same winter the Athenians in Sicily made a landing from their ships in the territory of Himera, in concert with the Sicels, who had invaded its borders from the interior, and also sailed to the islands of Aeolus. On their return to Rhegium they found the Athenian general Pythodorus, son of Isolochus, had come to relieve Laches in command of the fleet. The allies in Sicily had sailed to Athens and induced the Athenians to send out more ships to their aid, pointing out that the Syracusans, who already had control of the land, were making efforts to put together a navy, to avoid being any longer kept off the sea by a few ships. The Athenians proceeded to man forty ships to send them, thinking the war in Sicily would thus be ended sooner, and also wanting to give their navy practice. One of the generals, Pythodorus, was accordingly sent out with a few ships; Sophocles, son of Sostratides, and Eurymedon, son of Thucles, were to follow with the main body. Meanwhile Pythodorus had taken command of Laches’ ships, and toward the end of winter sailed against the Locrian fort that Laches had previously taken, and returned after being defeated in battle by the Locrians.

In the first days of the spring, the stream of fire issued from Etna, as on previous occasions, and destroyed some of the land of the Catanians, who live on Mount Etna, the largest mountain in Sicily. Fifty years, it is said, had passed since the previous eruption — there having been three in all since the Hellenes have inhabited Sicily. Such were the events of this winter; and with it ended the sixth year of this war of which Thucydides was the historian.
